units.title: Dynamic Programming II: Two Dimensions
units.tagline: Two indices, a table, and a fill order that respects the recurrence.
units.why:
The step from 1-D to 2-D is smaller than it looks: the procedure is identical,
and only the state gains an index. What changes is that the fill order now
matters in two directions at once, and that most of these problems compare **two
sequences** — where the recurrence always has the same shape.

Edit distance and longest common subsequence are worth real time. They are the
templates for a whole family (diff tools, spell-checkers, DNA alignment), they
are asked constantly, and once one of them is genuinely understood the others
fall out as small variations.
units.model:
### Two sequences: the universal shape

`dp[i][j]` = the answer for the first i characters of `a` and the first j of
`b`. Then:

```java
if (a.charAt(i - 1) == b.charAt(j - 1))
    dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j - 1] + 1;                  // characters match
else
    dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1]);  // drop one from either
```

That is longest common subsequence. Edit distance is the same table with a
different else-branch — the three operations, each costing one:

```java
dp[i][j] = 1 + Math.min(dp[i - 1][j - 1],       // replace
                Math.min(dp[i - 1][j],          // delete from a
                         dp[i][j - 1]));        // insert into a
```

**Use 1-based indices for the table and 0-based for the strings.** `dp[0][j]`
and `dp[i][0]` are then the empty-prefix base cases, which for edit distance are
`i` and `j` — deleting everything. That offset removes every boundary special
case, and the `- 1` in the character access is the price.

### Grid DP

`dp[i][j]` = the answer for the cell `(i, j)`, built from the cells you are
allowed to arrive from:

```java
dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j] + dp[i][j - 1];        // paths from above and from the left
```

The first row and column are the base cases. Fill top-to-bottom, left-to-right,
and every entry read is already done.

### Subset sum / 0-1 knapsack

`dp[i][w]` = can the first i items reach exactly w? Rolled to one dimension it
is the 1-D unit's descending loop:

```java
boolean[] dp = new boolean[target + 1];
dp[0] = true;
for (int x : nums)
    for (int w = target; w >= x; w--)       // DESCENDING ⇒ each item used once
        dp[w] |= dp[w - x];
```

The descending order is the entire 0/1 constraint, in one character.

### Intervals over a string

Palindromic problems are indexed by **(start, end)** and must be filled by
increasing length, because `dp[i][j]` depends on `dp[i+1][j-1]` — a shorter
interval:

```java
for (int len = 2; len <= n; len++)
    for (int i = 0; i + len - 1 < n; i++) {
        int j = i + len - 1;
        dp[i][j] = s.charAt(i) == s.charAt(j) && (len == 2 || dp[i + 1][j - 1]);
    }
```

Iterating i ascending and j ascending would read cells that are not yet
computed. When a recurrence points *inwards*, iterate by length.

### When the table is too big

Longest increasing subsequence has an O(n²) DP — for each i, scan every j < i —
but also an O(n log n) solution: keep the smallest possible tail for each length
and binary-search the position of each new element. The array is **not** the
subsequence; it only gives the correct length. That is the pattern to know:
sometimes a DP is replaced by a cleverer structure rather than optimised.

### Rolling to one row

If `dp[i][*]` only reads `dp[i-1][*]`, keep two rows — or one, if the reads go
in a direction that does not clobber what you still need. Same advice as in 1-D:
correctness first, space second.

pitfalls.cause: It is a per-length minimum tail, not a real subsequence.
pitfalls.fix: Only its length is the answer; reconstructing the sequence needs predecessor links.

pitfalls.symptom: `MemoryLimitExceeded` on a large two-sequence DP
pitfalls.cause: The full n × m table was allocated when only two rows are ever read.
pitfalls.fix: Roll to two rows — but only once the full version is correct.

checks.q: What do LCS and edit distance have in common?
checks.a: The same `dp[i][j]` over prefixes of two strings and the same match case. Only the mismatch branch differs: a max of two neighbours versus 1 + a min of three.

checks.q: Why use a 1-based table with 0-based strings?
checks.a: Row 0 and column 0 then represent the empty prefixes, which are the base cases. Every boundary special case disappears; the cost is the `- 1` in `charAt`.

checks.q: Why must interval DP be filled by increasing length?
checks.a: `dp[i][j]` depends on `dp[i+1][j-1]` — a strictly shorter interval — so all shorter intervals must already be computed.

checks.q: What does the LIS tails array actually contain?
checks.a: For each length, the smallest possible final value of an increasing subsequence of that length. Its size is the LIS length, but its contents are not necessarily a subsequence of the input.

checks.q: Ascending versus descending inner loop in a rolled knapsack — what is the difference?
checks.a: Ascending lets an item be reused within the same pass (unbounded); descending reads only the previous item's values, enforcing one use (0/1).

units.interview:
Two-sequence DP is asked constantly and is one of the few places where being
able to *draw the table* wins the interview. Fill a 3×3 example by hand while
explaining the three neighbours as replace, delete and insert; it takes ninety
seconds and it proves the recurrence in a way that code cannot. Offer the
rolled-row space optimisation at the end, after the table is right.

units.title: Tries (Prefix Trees)
units.tagline: When the structure of the key is the structure of the index.
units.why:
A hash map answers *"is this exact key present?"*. It cannot answer *"how many
keys start with `pre`?"*, because hashing deliberately destroys the relationship
between similar keys. A trie keeps it: the path from the root spells the key, so
every prefix is a node and prefix questions become a walk.

It is the final unit because it makes the curriculum's closing point — that
choosing the right structure *is* the algorithm. Autocomplete, dictionary
lookup, wildcard matching and even maximum-XOR (a trie over bits) are all the
same fifteen lines with a different walk.

signals.why: Prefix questions are what a hash map cannot answer.
The flag distinguishes a key from a mere prefix.
Recurse into every child at a wildcard.

signals.reach_for: Trie, stop at the first `word` node
signals.why: The shortest matching prefix is the first flag you meet.

signals.when: “longest word built one letter at a time”
signals.why: Every prefix must itself be a key.
O(32n) instead of O(n²).

skeletons.name: The trie
skeletons.when: Insert, search, and prefix search — the whole structure.
skeletons.note: One walk, three questions — the difference is only what you read at the end.

skeletons.name: Wildcard search
skeletons.when: `.` matching any single character.
skeletons.note: The wildcard branch is the only place the walk becomes a search.

skeletons.name: Shortest matching root
skeletons.when: Replace words by their dictionary root.
skeletons.note: Returning at the first `word` node is what makes it the shortest root.

skeletons.name: Bit trie for maximum XOR
skeletons.when: Maximum XOR pair, in O(32n).
skeletons.note: Greedy from the most significant bit: a higher bit outweighs everything below it.

costs.note: L = key length; independent of how many keys are stored.
Why the wildcard count is bounded.

pitfalls.symptom: A prefix is reported as a stored word
pitfalls.cause: The `word` flag is missing, so any reachable node looks like a key.
pitfalls.fix: Set `word = true` only at the final node of an insert.

pitfalls.symptom: `NullPointerException` while walking
pitfalls.cause: A child was dereferenced before being checked for null.
pitfalls.fix: Test for null immediately after each descent.

pitfalls.symptom: Memory blows up
pitfalls.cause: 26 pointers per node, times every node, on a large dictionary.
pitfalls.fix: Use a `Map<Character, Node>` for sparse or large alphabets.

pitfalls.symptom: The wildcard search is exponential
pitfalls.cause: Every `.` branches into 26 children.
pitfalls.fix: It is inherent; the problem bounds the wildcard count. Prune by depth where you can.

pitfalls.symptom: The root returned is not the shortest
pitfalls.cause: The walk continued past a `word` node looking for a longer match.
pitfalls.fix: Return at the first flag encountered.

pitfalls.symptom: Bit trie built from the least significant bit
pitfalls.cause: The greedy choice then optimises the wrong end of the number.
pitfalls.fix: Insert and query from bit 31 down — high bits dominate the value.

checks.q: What can a trie answer that a hash map cannot?
checks.a: Anything about prefixes — counts, autocomplete, longest matching root, wildcards. Hashing deliberately destroys the relationship between similar keys.

checks.q: Why does a trie node need a `word` flag?
checks.a: A node marks a position in the tree, not necessarily a stored key. Without the flag, inserting “car” would make “ca” appear to be a word.

checks.q: What is the cost of a trie lookup, and what is it *independent* of?
checks.a: O(L) in the key's length, independent of the number of keys stored. A million words does not slow it down.

checks.q: Why is the greedy walk correct for maximum XOR?
checks.a: Bits are inserted most-significant first, and a single higher bit outweighs every lower bit combined. So taking the opposite bit whenever it exists is always optimal.

units.interview:
Naming the trie is most of the marks — it is the expected answer for
autocomplete and dictionary problems, and candidates who have not met it tend to
propose scanning every word. Be ready for the trade-off question: a trie costs
far more memory than a hash set, so it earns its place only when prefixes,
wildcards or bit-greedy walks are actually needed.
